walkthroughs.title: Chest pressure on exertion

doorway: Presents to the family medicine clinic with chest pressure.
Vital signs are supplied at this station.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, and discuss your plan with the patient.

plan.notice: New exertional pressure with a falling activity threshold deserves urgent assessment even in a young adult and even when pain stops at rest.
plan.anchor: Change in threshold, not simply rest versus exertion
plan.pivot: Compare what activity triggered the first episode with what triggers it now. Ask whether symptoms are present now before a long history.
plan.exam: Listen at four cardiac sites on skin, compare posterior lung fields, and assess circulation. A reassuring resting examination does not exclude ischemia.
plan.avoid: Calling this stable angina solely because rest relieves it; assuming young age rules out coronary disease.

goals: Ask explicitly whether she is on aspirin. It changes the plan and it is the kind of detail a differential-with-a-plan lives on.
Quantify the tobacco history in pack-years rather than 'she smokes' - the rubric asks for specific documentation.
Ask about cocaine by name in a chest pain case; 'do you use drugs' is easy to answer no to.
walkthroughs.variant_guidance: Use this core presentation to learn the sequence before transferring to a variation.

timeline.student: I recommend urgent hospital evaluation because the pressure is happening with less activity than before. A heart problem is one possibility, and being comfortable now does not settle it. We should call emergency transport; please do not drive or exert yourself.

timeline.why: Proposed care, not a record of tests or treatment already completed.

timeline.student: What questions do you have about the next steps?

timeline.student: Heart disease is one important possibility, especially with this changing pattern and your family history. I cannot confirm the cause here. I recommend emergency assessment now, without driving yourself, so the team can check promptly and advise you about work safely.
timeline.patient: Understood.
timeline.why: Answer the concern that was just expressed. Give a defensible recommendation and explain uncertainty; do not promise a diagnosis or recovery before the evidence supports it.

note.S:
CC: Exertional chest pressure, 3 weeks.
HPI: 30-year-old woman with progressive substernal pressure, now triggered by one flight of stairs instead of heavier exertion. Episodes last about 5 minutes, 6/10, radiate to left arm/jaw and resolve with rest. Associated dyspnea, sweating and nausea. No rest pain, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, PND or edema. Not pleuritic, positional or meal-related; antacids ineffective. No similar prior episodes. Worried about her heart and missed work.
PMH: HTN, familial hypercholesterolemia, prediabetes. PSH: Appendectomy at 20; no subsequent admission.
Meds: Lisinopril 20 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg nightly; no aspirin. NKDA.
SH: Warehouse supervisor; smokes 1 pack/day since 18; 2–3 beers most evenings; no recreational drugs. Little exercise; frequent takeout.
FH: Father died of MI at 41; mother has HTN/diabetes; brother has inherited high cholesterol.
ROS: CV as above. Respiratory: no cough, hemoptysis or wheeze. GI: nausea; no heartburn, vomiting or abdominal pain. LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected, not tested.
P: 1. Arrange EMS transfer now; obtain ECG promptly and serial troponin through the emergency team without delaying transfer. Review allergy, bleeding and hemodynamics before clinician-directed aspirin/anti-ischemic therapy. Explain the worsening exertional pattern, avoid exertion and do not drive; defer stress testing and OMT until ACS is excluded.

2. Obtain echocardiography with Doppler if valve disease remains suspected; cardiology review alongside the ischemia assessment. Avoid heavy exertion pending assessment; explain to report faintness or worsening dyspnea immediately.

3. After urgent causes are excluded, review reflux symptoms and consider an acid-suppression trial; counsel on tobacco cessation and avoiding late meals. Arrange primary-care follow-up after emergency assessment; antacid relief would not exclude ischemia.

differentials.name: Stable angina pectoris
differentials.not_most_likely_because: The 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline draws the acute/stable line on CHANGE, not on whether pain occurs at rest: 'stable' is reserved for symptoms that are chronic with consistent precipitants. Her symptoms are three weeks old and the threshold has fallen from heavy exertion to one flight of stairs - one flight of stairs is the operational definition of CCS class III. That makes this new-onset angina of at least CCS III AND crescendo angina, two of the three accepted unstable-angina presentations, neither of which requires rest pain. Absence of rest pain is the commonest reasoning error on this case; it is not reassurance.

differentials.name: Stable angina pectoris
differentials.not_most_likely_because: The 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline draws the acute/stable line on CHANGE, not on whether pain occurs at rest: 'stable' is reserved for symptoms that are chronic with consistent precipitants. Her symptoms are three weeks old and the threshold has fallen from heavy exertion to one flight of stairs - one flight of stairs is the operational definition of CCS class III. That makes this new-onset angina of at least CCS III AND crescendo angina, two of the three accepted unstable-angina presentations, neither of which requires rest pain. Absence of rest pain is the commonest reasoning error on this case; it is not reassurance.

omissions: Ask explicitly whether she is on aspirin. It changes the plan and it is the kind of detail a differential-with-a-plan lives on.
Quantify the tobacco history in pack-years rather than 'she smokes' - the rubric asks for specific documentation.
Ask about cocaine by name in a chest pain case; 'do you use drugs' is easy to answer no to.
Palpate the chest wall deliberately and say what you are testing for. The value of this maneuver is the NEGATIVE, and a negative you can document is worth as much as a positive.
Ask what she thinks is going on before reassuring her. Her answer is the F.I.F.E. item, and it is also the reason she finally came in.

note.S:
CC: Exertional chest pressure, 3 weeks.
HPI: 30-year-old woman with progressive substernal pressure, now triggered by one flight of stairs instead of heavier exertion. Episodes last about 5 minutes, 6/10, radiate to left arm/jaw and resolve with rest. Associated dyspnea, sweating and nausea. No rest pain, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, PND or edema. Not pleuritic, positional or meal-related; antacids ineffective. No similar prior episodes. Worried about her heart and missed work.
PMH: HTN, familial hypercholesterolemia, prediabetes. PSH: Appendectomy at 20; no subsequent admission.
Meds: Lisinopril 20 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg nightly; no aspirin. NKDA.
SH: Warehouse supervisor; smokes 1 pack/day since 18; 2–3 beers most evenings; no recreational drugs. Little exercise; frequent takeout.
FH: Father died of MI at 41; mother has HTN/diabetes; brother has inherited high cholesterol.
ROS: CV as above. Respiratory: no cough, hemoptysis or wheeze. GI: nausea; no heartburn, vomiting or abdominal pain. LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected, not tested.
Care needs: I am worried about getting to follow-up and knowing whom to call if I get worse.
P: 1. Arrange EMS transfer now; obtain ECG promptly and serial troponin through the emergency team without delaying transfer. Review allergy, bleeding and hemodynamics before clinician-directed aspirin/anti-ischemic therapy. Explain the worsening exertional pattern, avoid exertion and do not drive; defer stress testing and OMT until ACS is excluded. Confirm transport and a practical contact for deterioration.

2. Obtain echocardiography with Doppler if valve disease remains suspected; cardiology review alongside the ischemia assessment. Avoid heavy exertion pending assessment; explain to report faintness or worsening dyspnea immediately.

3. After urgent causes are excluded, review reflux symptoms and consider an acid-suppression trial; counsel on tobacco cessation and avoiding late meals. Arrange primary-care follow-up after emergency assessment; antacid relief would not exclude ischemia.

reasoning.question: Has the pressure changed in frequency, duration or the activity needed to trigger it?
reasoning.why: A worsening pattern can raise concern for an acute coronary process.
reasoning.if_present: New/worsening or rest symptoms require urgent assessment.
reasoning.if_absent: An unchanged exertional pattern still needs cardiac risk assessment; absence of pain now is not exclusion.
reasoning.next_action: Establish current symptoms, vitals and ECG access before routine counseling.
reasoning.document: Record the answer and findings only if obtained; keep possible diagnoses in Assessment and proposed investigations in Plan.

differentials.name: Stable angina pectoris
differentials.not_most_likely_because: The 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline draws the acute/stable line on CHANGE, not on whether pain occurs at rest: 'stable' is reserved for symptoms that are chronic with consistent precipitants. Her symptoms are three weeks old and the threshold has fallen from heavy exertion to one flight of stairs - one flight of stairs is the operational definition of CCS class III. That makes this new-onset angina of at least CCS III AND crescendo angina, two of the three accepted unstable-angina presentations, neither of which requires rest pain. Absence of rest pain is the commonest reasoning error on this case; it is not reassurance.

omissions: Ask explicitly whether she is on aspirin. It changes the plan and it is the kind of detail a differential-with-a-plan lives on.
Quantify the tobacco history in pack-years rather than 'she smokes' - the rubric asks for specific documentation.
Ask about cocaine by name in a chest pain case; 'do you use drugs' is easy to answer no to.
Palpate the chest wall deliberately and say what you are testing for. The value of this maneuver is the NEGATIVE, and a negative you can document is worth as much as a positive.
Ask what she thinks is going on before reassuring her. Her answer is the F.I.F.E. item, and it is also the reason she finally came in.

recall.prompt: Before naming a diagnosis, what is the key distinction in this presentation?
recall.answer: Compare what activity triggered the first episode with what triggers it now. Ask whether symptoms are present now before a long history.

recall.prompt: Which specific examination or safety step changes what you can document?
recall.answer: Listen at four cardiac sites on skin, compare posterior lung fields, and assess circulation. A reassuring resting examination does not exclude ischemia.

recall.prompt: Name one tempting documentation or reasoning error and how you will prevent it.
recall.answer: Calling this stable angina solely because rest relieves it; assuming young age rules out coronary disease.
